title: Completeness and soundness amplification in StoqMA
formal: For every pair of efficiently computable threshold functions \(a(n),b(n)\) with \(1/2\le b(n)<a(n)\le 1\) and \(a(n)- b(n)\ge 1/q(n)\) for some polynomial q, and every integer-valued polynomial \(\ell\)\((n)\ge 2\), is \(StoqMA(a,b)\) contained in \(StoqMA(1- 2^{- \ell (n)}, 1/2+2^{- \ell (n)})\)? Here n is the classical input length. The new verifier must remain in the same one-witness stoquastic circuit model, with polynomially many gates, witness qubits and ancillas.
context:
The computation is classically reversible, but its ancillas and final measurement allow a nonnegative quantum witness to affect acceptance. This restricted verification model arises in the complexity of stoquastic local Hamiltonians. Familiar error-reduction statements for unrestricted quantum verification do not automatically give the required stoquastic verifier.

The source’s Theorem 5 maps thresholds \((1/2+u/2,1/2+v/2)\) to \((1/2+u^{r}/2,1/2+v^{r}/2)\) for polynomial r. This improves excess soundness but can also lower completeness. Conjecture 6 asks for simultaneous amplification towards completeness one and soundness one half.

The 2025 published paper proves that negligible completeness error with a suitable inverse-polynomial gap is already contained in MA, the class of promise problems verified in polynomial time with a classical witness and random bits. Its Corollary 1.5 makes general StoqMA error reduction equivalent to StoqMA=MA.

The July 2026 preprint still explicitly calls general one-witness error reduction open. Its restricted repetition results do not supply the two threshold limits required here for arbitrary original completeness.

The May 2026 preprint claims that the number of stoquastic provers can be reduced while retaining an inverse-polynomial gap. It explicitly avoids assuming general amplification. This preprint claim is not recorded as a solution of the one-witness error-reduction question.
why: Would determine whether the stoquastic verification model has ordinary exponential error reduction and, through the published equivalence, whether its proof power collapses to classical Merlin–Arthur verification.
status_note: Read Conjecture 6, the verifier definition and soundness-only theorem, the 2025 published equivalence, and the relevant statements in the May and July 2026 preprints. No full one-witness amplification theorem was found through 12 September 2026. The July 2026 source explicitly still calls the general question open.

sentences: A StoqMA verifier uses classical reversible gates, special initial ancillas and one final measurement in the plus/minus basis.
It accepts a suitable nonnegative quantum witness on yes instances and must reject arbitrary witnesses with the prescribed soundness bound on no instances.
The question asks whether every inverse-polynomial gap can be amplified to completeness exponentially close to one and soundness exponentially close to one half.
Soundness-only repetition is known, but it does not provide this simultaneous improvement.
A published theorem makes full error reduction equivalent to StoqMA=MA, and July 2026 work still states the general problem as open.

definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}},\mathrm{L}_{no})\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings, with no required answer outside their union. Membership in \(StoqMA(a,b)\) means there is a deterministic polynomial-time procedure which, given x of length n, produces a verification circuit \(V_{x}\) on \(m(n)+r(n)+s(n)\) qubits, all counts polynomially bounded in n. Its initial state is |\(w\rangle \otimes |0\rangle ^{\otimes r}\otimes |+\rangle ^{\otimes s}\), where |+⟩=\((|0\rangle +|1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) and the m-qubit witness has norm one. The circuit uses only classical reversible gates: NOT flips a bit, CNOT flips its target if its control is one, and Toffoli flips its target if both controls are one. These gates act linearly on computational-basis states. There are no intermediate measurements or arbitrary quantum gates. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the \(\{|+\rangle ,|- \rangle\}\) basis, with |−⟩=\((|0\rangle - |1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\), and outcome + means acceptance. Its acceptance probability is the squared norm after projection onto |+⟩ on that qubit. If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness with real nonnegative computational-basis amplitudes must be accepted with probability at least \(a(n)\). If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{no}\), every normalized witness, including arbitrary complex amplitudes, must be accepted with probability at most \(b(n)\). The source proves that a maximizing witness can be chosen nonnegative. Efficient threshold computability is understood in the standard precision sense: their values can be approximated within \(2^{- t}\) in time polynomial in \(n+t\). The inverse-polynomial gap permits this conventional representation. Class containment quantifies over promise problems and asserts existence of new uniform verifiers; it does not demand a blackbox compiler acting on an arbitrary verifier description. Polynomial bounds of the new verifier may depend on the original verifier, q and \(\ell\). Soundness approaches \(1/2\) from above, not zero; the requested improvement is relative to the stoquastic acceptance baseline.
answer_criterion: Prove the containment for every admissible a,b and \(\ell\), or refute this universally quantified amplification statement. A positive answer must achieve both exponentially small completeness error and exponentially small excess soundness above \(1/2\) while retaining the allowed gates, initial ancillas and final measurement. Soundness-only repetition, perfect-completeness special cases, extra destructive-interference gates, or additional unentangled provers do not establish the claim.
